n: *Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the days of” (so KJV, NASB, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “O peoples, all of them.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “O earth and that which fills it”; cf. KJV “and all that therein is.”

*Text-critical note:* The MT has the jussive form verb וִיהִי (vihi, “may he be”), while the Dead Sea Scrolls have the imperfect form יהיה (yihyeh, “he will be”). The LXX uses a future indicative. On the basis of distance from the primary accent, GKC 325-26 §109.*k* attempts to explain the form as a rhythmical shortening of the imperfect rather than a true jussive. Some of the examples in GKC may now be explained as preterites, while others are text-critical problems. And some may have other modal explanations. But other examples are not readily explained by these considerations. The text-critical decision and the grammatical explanation in GKC would both lead to translating as an imperfect. Some translations render it in a jussive sense, either as request: “And let my Lord God be your accuser” (NJPS), or as dependent purpose/result: “that the Sovereign Lord may bear witness against you” (NIV11).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Lord from his majestic palace.” The verb is supplied from the previous line by the convention of ellipsis and double duty. Cf. CEV “the Lord God accuses you from his holy temple,” TEV “He speaks from his holy temple.”

*Translator's note:* Or “his holy temple” (KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT). This refers to the Lord’s dwelling in heaven, however, rather than the temple in Jerusalem (note the following verse, which describes a theophany).

*Translator's note:* Or “For look.” The expression כִּי־הִנֵּה (ki-hinneh) may function as an explanatory introduction (“For look!”; {{Isaiah 26:21|Isa 26:21}}; {{Isaiah 60:2|60:2}}; {{Isaiah 65:17|65:17}}, {{Isaiah 65:18|18}}: {{Isaiah 66:15|66:15}}; Jer 1:15; 25:29; 30:10; 45:5; 46:27; 50:9; {{Ezekiel 30:9|Ezek 30:9}}; {{Ezekiel 36:9|36:9}}; Zech 2:10; 3:8), or as an emphatic introduction (“Look!”; {{Judges 3:15|Jdgs 3:15}}; {{Isaiah 3:1|Isa 3:1}}; Jer 8:17; 30:3; 49:15; Hos 9:6; Joel 3:1 [4:1 HT]; {{Amos 4:2|Amos 4:2}}, {{Amos 4:13|13}}; {{Amos 6:11|6:11}}, {{Amos 6:14|14}}; {{Amos 9:9|9:9}}; {{Habakkuk 1:6|Hab 1:6}}; Zech 2:9 [2:13 HT]; Zech 3:9; 11:16).

*Translator's note:* Or “high places” (KJV, NASB, NIV84, NRSV, NLT); NIV11 “heights.”

*Translator's note:* Or “melt” (NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT). This is a figurative description of earthquakes, landslides, and collapse of the mountains, rather than some sort of volcanic activity (note the remainder of the verse).

*Translator's note:* Or “rupture.” This may refer to the appearance of a valley after the blockage of a landslide has effectively divided it.

*Study note:* Jacob is an alternate name for Israel (see {{Genesis 32:28|Gen 32:28}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and because of.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “house.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Is it not Samaria?” The capital city, Samaria, represents the policies of the government and trend-setting behaviors of her people. The rhetorical question expects a positive answer, “Yes, it is.”

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads, “What are Judah’s high places?” while the LXX, Syriac, and Targum read, “What is Judah’s sin?” Whether or not the original text was “sin,” the passage certainly alludes to Judah’s sin as a complement to Samaria’s. “High places” are where people worshiped idols; they could, by metonymy, represent pagan worship. Smith notes, however, that, “Jerusalem was not known for its high places,” and so follows the LXX as representing the original text (R. Smith, *Micah* [WBC], 16). Given the warning in v. {{Micah 1:3|3}} that the Lord will march on the land’s high places (“mountain tops,” based on the same word but a different plural form), this may be a way of referring to that threat while evoking the notion of idolatry.

*Translator's note:* Jerusalem, the capital of Judah, represents the nation’s behavior. The rhetorical question expects an affirmative answer.

*Study note:* In vv. {{Micah 1:2|2-5}} Micah narrows the scope of God’s judgment from the nations (vv. {{Micah 1:2|2-4}}) to his covenant people (v. {{Micah 1:5|5}}). Universal judgment is coming, but ironically Israel is the focal point of God’s anger. In v. {{Micah 1:5|5c}} the prophet includes Judah within the scope of divine judgment, for Judah has followed in the pagan steps of the northern kingdom. He accomplishes this with rhetorical skill. In v. {{Micah 1:5|5b}} he develops the first assertion of v. {{Micah 1:5|5a}} (“All of this is because of Jacob’s rebellion”). One expects in v. {{Micah 1:5|5c}} an elaboration of the second assertion in v. {{Micah 1:5|5a}} (“and the sins of the nation of Israel”), which one assumes, in light of v. {{Micah 1:5|5b}}, pertains to the northern kingdom. But the prophet makes it clear that “the nation of Israel” includes Judah. Verses {{Micah 1:6|6-7}} further develop v. {{Micah 1:5|5b}} (judgment on the northern kingdom), while vv. {{Micah 1:8|8-16}} expand on v. {{Micah 1:5|5c}} (judgment on Judah).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “her stones.” The term “stones” is a metonymy for the city walls whose foundations were constructed of stone masonry.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will uncover her foundations.” The term “foundations” refers to the lower courses of the stones of the city’s outer fortification walls.

*Study note:* The precious metal used by Samaria’s pagan worship centers to make idols is compared to a prostitute’s wages because Samaria had been unfaithful to the Lord and prostituted herself to pagan gods such as Baal.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and all her prostitute’s wages will be burned with fire.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will make desolate” (so NASB).

*Translator's note:* Or “for” (KJV, NASB, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* No object is specified in the Hebrew text; the words “the metal” are supplied from the context.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for from a prostitute’s wages she gathered, and to a prostitute’s wages they will return.” When the metal was first collected it was comparable to the coins a prostitute would receive for her services. The metal was then formed into idols, but now the Lord’s fiery judgment would reduce the metal images to their original condition.

*Translator's note:* The prophet is probably the speaker here.

*Translator's note:* Or “stripped.” The precise meaning of this Hebrew word is unclear. It may refer to walking barefoot (see {{2 Samuel 15:30|2 Sam 15:30}}) or to partially stripping oneself (see {{Job 12:17|Job 12:17-19}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “naked.” This probably does not refer to complete nudity, but to stripping off one’s outer garments as an outward sign of the destitution felt by the mourner.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will make lamentation.”

*Translator's note:* Or “a jackal”; CEV “howling wolves.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[make] a mourning.”

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps “ostrich” (cf. ASV, NAB, NASB, NRSV, NLT).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “her.”

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads the plural “wounds/plagues”; the singular is read by the LXX, Syriac, and Vg.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “come to.”

*Translator's note:* Or “reached.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the gate.” Kings and civic leaders typically conducted important business at the city gate (see {{1 Kings 22:10|1 Kgs 22:10}} for an example), and the term is understood here to refer by metonymy to the leadership who would be present at the gate.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Tell it not in Gath.” The Hebrew word for “tell” (נָגַד, nagad) sounds like the name of the city, Gath (גַּת, gat).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew infinitive absolute before the negated jussive emphasizes the prohibition.

*Study note:* The name *Beth Leaphrah* means “house of dust.”

*Text-critical note:* The translation assumes a masculine plural imperative. If one were to emend בְּבֵית (bevet) to בֵית (vet), Beth Leaphrah would then be the addressee and the feminine singular imperative (see *Qere*) could be retained, “O Beth Leaphrah, sit in the dust.”

*Translator's note:* Or “wallow.” The verb פָּלַשׁ (palash, “roll about [in dust])” refers to a cultural behavior associated with mourning.

*Translator's note:* The feminine singular participle is here used in a collective sense for all the residents of the town. See GKC 394 §122.*s*.

*Study note:* The place name *Shaphir* means “pleasant” in Hebrew.

*Study note:* The place name *Zaanan* sounds like the verb “go out” in Hebrew.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “have not gone out.” NIV “will not come out”; NLT “dare not come outside.”

*Study note:* The place name *Beth Ezel* means “house of nearness” or “house of proximity” in Hebrew.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the lamentation of Beth Ezel.” The following words could be the lamentation offered up by Beth Ezel (subjective genitive) or the mourning song sung over it (objective genitive).

*Translator's note:* The precise meaning of the line is uncertain. The translation assumes: (a) the subject of the third masculine singular verb יִקַּח (yiqqakh, “he/it takes”) is the conqueror, (b) the second masculine plural suffix (“you”) on the preposition מִן (min, “from”) refers to the residents of Shaphir and Zaanan, (c) the final form עֶמְדָּתוֹ should be emended to חֲמַדְּתוֹ, “his (the conqueror’s) desire.”

*Text-critical note:* The form עֶמְדָּתוֹ (ʿemdato) should be emended to חֲמַדְּתוֹ (khamadto, “his (the conqueror’s) desire”).

*Study note:* The place name *Maroth* sounds like the Hebrew word for “bitter.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[the residents of Maroth] writhe [= “anxiously long for”?] good.”

*Text-critical note:* The translation assumes an emendation of חָלָה (khalah; from חִיל, khil, “to writhe”) to יִחֲלָה (yikhalah; from יָחַל, yakhal, “to wait”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “though disaster has come down from the Lord to the gate of Jerusalem.”

*Study note:* The place name *Lachish* sounds like the Hebrew word for “team [of horses].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “she”; this has been translated as second person (“you”) in keeping with the direct address to the residents of Lachish in the previous line.

*Study note:* The epithet *Daughter Zion* pictures the city of Jerusalem as a young lady.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “She was the beginning of sin for Daughter Zion.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for in you was found the transgressions of Israel.”

*Translator's note:* The subject of the feminine singular verb is probably Lachish.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you will give a dowry to”; NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV “give parting gifts to.” Lachish is compared to a father who presents wedding gifts to his daughter as she leaves her father’s home to take up residence with her husband. In similar fashion Lachish will bid farewell to Moresheth Gath, for the latter will be taken by the invader.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “houses.” By metonymy this refers to the people who live in them.

*Study note:* The place name *Achzib* (אַכְזִיב, ʾakhziv, “place on the dried up river”; see *HALOT* 45 s.v. אַכְזָב) creates a word play on the similar sounding term כָּזָב (kazav, “lie, deception”; *HALOT* 468 s.v. כָּזָב). Like the dried up river upon which its name was based, the city of Achzib would fail to help the kings of Israel in their time of need.

*Translator's note:* Or “will be a deception.” The term אַכְזָב (ʾakhzav) is often translated “deception,” derived from the verb I כָּזָב (“to deceive, lie”; *HALOT* 467-68 s.v. I כזב). However, it probably means “what is dried up,” since (1) the noun elsewhere refers to an empty well or dried river in summer (Jer 15:18; cf. {{Job 6:15|Job 6:15-20}}) (*HALOT* 45 s.v. אַכְזָב); (2) the place-name “Achzib” (אַכְזִיב) literally means “place on the אַכְזָב [dried up river]” (*HALOT* 45 s.v. אַכְזָב); and (3) it is derived from the verb II כָּזָב (“to dry up [brook]”; {{Isaiah 58:11|Isa 58:11}}), which also appears in Mishnaic Hebrew and Arabic. The point of the metaphor is that Achzib will be as disappointing to the kings of Israel as a dried up spring in the summer is to a thirsty traveler in the Jordanian desert.

*Study note:* Because of the enemy invasion, *Achzib* would not be able to deliver soldiers for the army and/or services normally rendered to the crown.

*Study note:* The place name *Mareshah* sounds like the Hebrew word for “conqueror.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Again a conqueror I will bring to you, residents of Mareshah.” The first person verb is problematic, for the Lord would have to be the subject (cf. NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT). But the prophet appears to be delivering this lament and the Lord is referred to in the third person in v. {{Micah 1:12|12}}. Consequently many emend the verb to a third person form (יָבוֹא, yavoʾ) and understand the “conqueror” as subject.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to Adullam the glory of Israel will go.” This probably means that the nation’s leadership will run for their lives and, like David of old, hide from their enemy in the caves of Adullam. Cf. NIV84’s “He who is the glory of Israel will come to Adullam,” which sounds as if an individual is in view, and could be understood as a messianic reference. NIV11 translates “The nobles of Israel will flee to Adullam.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “over the sons of your delight.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “make wide your baldness.”

*Translator's note:* Or “a vulture” (cf. NIV, TEV); CEV “a buzzard.” The Hebrew term נֶשֶׁר (nesher) refers to the griffon vulture or eagle.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “those who think up evil.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “upon their beds.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “at the light of morning they do it.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they desire fields and rob [them], and houses and take [them] away.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and they oppress a man and his home.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and a man and his inheritance.” The verb עָשַׁק (ʿashaq, “to oppress”; “to wrong”) does double duty in the parallel structure and is understood by ellipsis in the second line.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “clan” or “extended family.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from which you will not remove your neck.” The words “It will be like a yoke” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* Or “you will not.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “one will lament [with] a lamentation [and] say.”

*Text-critical note:* The form נִהְיָה (nihyah) should be omitted as dittographic (note the preceding וְנָהָה נְהִי venahah nehi).

*Translator's note:* Or “exchange.” The LXX suggests a reading יִמַּד (yimmad) from מָדַד (madad, “to measure”). In this case one could translate, “the property of my people is measured out [i.e., for resale].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “how one removes for me.” Apparently the preposition has the nuance “from” here (cf. KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT).

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew term שׁוֹבֵב (shovev, “the one turning back”) elsewhere has the nuance “apostate” (cf. NASB) or “traitor” (cf. NIV). The translation assumes an emendation to שָׁבָה (shavah, “captor”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to the one turning back he assigns our fields.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “therefore you will not have one who strings out a measuring line by lot in the assembly of the Lord.”

*Study note:* *No one will assign you land in the Lord’s community*. When judgment passes and the people are restored to the land, those greedy ones who disregarded the ancient land allotments will not be allowed to participate in the future redistribution of the land.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “‘Do not foam at the mouth,’ they foam at the mouth.” The verb נָטַף (nataf) means “to drip.” When used of speech it probably has the nuance “to drivel, to foam at the mouth” (*HALOT* 694 s.v. נטף). The sinful people tell the Lord’s prophets not to “foam at the mouth,” which probably refers in a derogatory way to their impassioned style of delivery. But the Lord (who is probably still speaking here, see v. {{Micah 2:3|3}}) sarcastically refers to their impassioned exhortation as “foaming at the mouth.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they should not foam at the mouth concerning these things, humiliation will not be removed.”

*Text-critical note:* If one follows the MT as it stands, it would appear that the Lord here condemns the people for their “foaming at the mouth” and then announces that judgment is inevitable. The present translation assumes that this is a continuation of the quotation of what the people say. In this case the subject of “foam at the mouth” is the Lord’s prophets. In the second line יִסַּג (yissag, a Niphal imperfect from סוּג, sug, “to remove”) is emended to יַסִּגֵנוּ (yassigenu; a Hiphil imperfect from נָסַג/נָשַׂג, nasag/nasag, “to reach; to overtake”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “house” (so many English versions); CEV “descendants.’

*Text-critical note:* The MT has אָמוּר (ʾamur), an otherwise unattested passive participle, which is better emended to אָמוֹר (ʾamor), an infinitive absolute functioning as a finite verb (see BDB 55 s.v. אָמַר).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew word רוּחַ (ruakh) often means “Spirit” when used of the Lord, but here it seems to have an abstract sense, “patience.” See BDB 925 s.v. 3.d.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Has the patience of the Lord run short? Or are these his deeds?” The rhetorical questions expect the answer, “No, of course not.” The people contest the prophet’s claims that the Lord’s judgment is falling on the nation.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Do not my words accomplish good for the one who walks uprightly?” The rhetorical question expects the answer, “Of course they do!” The Lord begins his response to the claim of the house of Jacob that they are immune to judgment (see v. {{Micah 2:7|7a}}). He points out that the godly are indeed rewarded, but then he goes on to show that those in the house of Jacob are not godly and can expect divine judgment, not blessing (vv. {{Micah 2:8|8-11}}). Some emend “my words” to “his words.” In this case, v. {{Micah 2:7|7b}} is a continuation of the immediately preceding quotation. The people, thinking they are godly, confidently ask, “Do not his [God’s] words accomplish good for the one who walks uprightly?”

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “Recently my people rise up as an enemy.” The MT is problematic in light of v. {{Micah 2:9|9}}, where “my people” are the object of oppression, not the perpetrators of it. The form וְאֶתְמוּל (veʾetmul, “and recently”) is probably the product of fusion and subsequent suppression of an (ע) ʿayin. The translation assumes an emendation to וְאַתֶּם עַל (veʾattem ʿal, “and you against [my people]”). The second person plural pronoun fits well with the second plural verb forms of vv. {{Micah 2:8|8b-10}}. If this emendation is accepted, then יְקוֹמֵם (yeqomem, the Polel imperfect of קוּם [qum]) should be emended to קָמִים (qamim; a Qal participle from the same root).

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “From the front of a garment glory [or perhaps, “a robe”] you strip off,” but this makes little if any sense. The term מִמּוּל (mimmul, “from the front of”) is probably the product of dittography (note the preceding word, which ends in [ם] *mem*) and subsequent suppression of ע (ʿayin). The translation assumes an emendation to מֵעַל (meʿal, “from upon”). The translation also assumes an emendation of שַׂלְמָה אֶדֶר (salmah ʾeder, “a garment, glory [or robe]”) to שֹׁלְמִים אֲדֶרֶת (sholemim ʾaderet, “[from] a friend the robe [you strip off]”). The MT’s אֶדֶר (ʾeder) is the result of improper division (the article has erroneously been attached to the preceding word) and haplography (of the final *tav*, which also begins the following word).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from those passing by peacefully, returnees from war.” Actual refugees, however, are probably not in view. The second line compares those who pass by peacefully with individuals returning from war. The battle is over and they do not expect their own countrymen to attack them.

*Text-critical note:* The passive participle שׁוּבֵי (shuve) is unattested elsewhere and should be emended to a participle שָׁבִים (shavim).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “women.” This may be a synecdoche of the whole (women) for the part (widows).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “her little children” or “her infants”; ASV, NRSV “young children.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from their children you take my glory forever.” The yod (י) ending on הֲדָרִי (hadari) is usually taken as a first person common singular suffix (“my glory”). But it may be the archaic genitive ending (“glory of”) in the construct expression “glory of perpetuity,” that is, “perpetual glory.” In either case, this probably refers to the dignity or honor the Lord bestowed on each Israelite family by giving them a share of his land to be inherited perpetually from one generation to another within each family. The term הָדָר (hadar) may refer to possessions that a person prizes (Lam 1:6).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Arise and go!” These imperatives are rhetorical. Those who wrongly drove widows and orphans from their homes and land inheritances will themselves be driven out of the land (cf. {{Isaiah 5:8|Isa 5:8-17}}). This is an example of poetic justice.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for this is no resting place.” The Lord speaks to the oppressors.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “uncleanness will destroy, and destruction will be severe.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “if a man, coming [as] wind and falsehood, should lie”; NASB “walking after wind and falsehood”; NIV “a liar and a deceiver.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will foam at the mouth concerning wine and beer.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he would be the foamer at the mouth for this people.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the remnant of Israel.”

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads בָּצְרָה (batsrah, “Bozrah”) but the form should be emended to בַּצִּרָה (batsirah, “into the fold”). See D. R. Hillers, *Micah* (Hermeneia), 38.

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads “its pasture,” but the final vav (ו) belongs with the following verb. See GKC 413 §127.*i*.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and they will be noisy [or perhaps, “excited”] from men.” The subject of the third feminine plural verb תְּהִימֶנָה (tehimenah, “they will be noisy”) is probably the feminine singular צֹאן (tsoʾn, “flock”). (For another example of this collective singular noun with a feminine plural verb, see {{Genesis 30:38|Gen 30:38}}.) In the construction מֵאָדָם (meʾadam, “from men”) the preposition is probably causal. L. C. Allen translates “bleating in fear of men” (*Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, and Micah* [NICOT], 300), but it is possible to take the causal sense as “because of the large quantity of men.” In this case the sheep metaphor and the underlying reality are mixed.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the one who breaks through goes up before them.” The verb form is understood as a perfect of certitude, emphasizing the certainty of this coming event.

*Study note:* The “fold” from which the sheep/people *break out* is probably a reference to their place of exile.

*Translator's note:* The three verb forms (a perfect and two preterites with vav [ו] consecutive) indicate certitude.

*Translator's note:* The verb form (a preterite with vav [ו] consecutive) indicates certitude.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Lord [will be] at their head.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “heads.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “house.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Should you not know justice?” The rhetorical question expects the answer, “Of course you should!”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the ones who.”

*Translator's note:* Or “good.”

*Translator's note:* Or “evil.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “their skin from upon them.” The referent of the pronoun (“my people,” referring to Jacob and/or the house of Israel, with the Lord as the speaker) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and their flesh from their bones.”

*Study note:* Micah compares the social injustice perpetrated by the house of Jacob/Israel to cannibalism because it threatens the very lives of the oppressed.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who.”

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads “and they chop up as in a pot.” The translation assumes an emendation of כַּאֲשֶׁר (ka’asher, “as”) to כִּשְׁאֵר (kishʾer, “like flesh”).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they,” referring to the indicted leaders in vv. {{Micah 3:1|1-3}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “concerning the prophets, those who mislead my people.” Some prefer to begin the quotation after “the Lord has said” (cf. NIV). But when the preposition עַל (ʿal, “about”) occurs with this introductory formula it regularly indicates who is being spoken about. (When a person is not the object of the preposition, it may begin the quote, meaning “because.”) Including the first person pronominal suffix (in “my people”) after a third person introduction may sound awkward, but also occurs in Jer 14:15; 23:2 (and perhaps Jer 12:14, a text critical question). Hillers prefers to add הוֹי (hoy, “woe, ah”) at the beginning of the quotation, after the graphically similar יְהוָה (yehvah; see D. R. Hillers, *Micah* [Hermeneia], 44). The phrase הוֹי עַל (hoy ʿal, “woe upon”) occurs in Jer 50:27 and {{Ezekiel 13:3|Ezek 13:3}} (with “the prophets” following the preposition in the latter instance).

From 6:1 the verse numbers in the English Bible and the Hebrew Bible are again the same.

*Study note:* In riddle-like fashion this verse alludes to David, as the references to Bethlehem and to his ancient origins/activities indicate. The passage anticipates the second coming of the great king to usher in a new era of national glory for Israel. Other prophets are more direct and name this coming ideal ruler “David” (Jer 30:9; {{Ezekiel 34:23|Ezek 34:23-24}}; {{Ezekiel 37:24|37:24-25}}; Hos 3:5). Of course, this prophecy of “David’s” second coming is actually fulfilled through his descendant, the Messiah, who will rule in the spirit and power of his famous ancestor and bring to realization the Davidic royal ideal in an even greater way than the historical David (see {{Isaiah 11:1|Isa 11:1}}, {{Isaiah 11:10|10}}; Jer 33:15).

These were to be burned or cut down ({{Deuteronomy 12:3|Deut 12:3}}; {{Deuteronomy 16:21|16:21}}; {{Judges 6:25|Judg 6:25}}, {{Judges 6:28|28}}, {{Judges 6:30|30}}; {{2 Kings 18:4|2 Kgs 18:4}}). *Text-critical note:* The MT reads, “Listen, tribe (or staff) and who appointed it.” Verse {{Micah 6:10|10}} then begins with עוֹד (ʿod, “still” or “again”). The LXX reads, “who will set the city in order?” The translation assumes an emendation of וּמִי יְעָדָהּ. עוֹד (umi yeʿadah. ʿod…, “and who appointed it. Possibly it is a combination of the interrogative particle and אִשׁ (ʾish), an alternate form of יֵשׁ (yesh, “there is/are”). One could then translate literally, “Are there treasures of sin [in] the house of the sinful?” The translation assumes an emendation to הַאֶשֶּׁה (haʾesheh, from נָשָׁא, nashaʾ, “to forget”), “Will I forget?” The rhetorical question expects an answer, “No, I will not forget.”

The translation assumes it is a Hiphal imperfect from נָסַג/נָשַׂג (nasag/nasag, “reach; overtake”) and that hunting imagery is employed. (Note the reference to hunger in the first line of the verse.) See D. R. Hillers, *Micah* (Hermeneia), 80.

Borowski, *Agriculture in Iron Age Israel*, 119. The Hebrew term דָּרַךְ (darakh) may have an idiomatic sense of “press” here, or perhaps the imagery of the following parallel line (referring to treading grapes) has dictated the word choice.

*Translator's note:* More literally, “the great one announces what his appetite desires and they weave it together.” Apparently this means that subordinates plot and maneuver to make sure the prominent man’s desires materialize.

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads יָשָׁר מִמְּסוּכָה (yashar mimmesukhah) “a godly [person] from a thorn bush.” Theoretically the preposition מִן (min, “from”) could be comparative (“more than”), but it would need an attributive adjective for this meaning. Most likely this is a case of wrong word division, where the מ (mem) is not מִן (min, “from”), but is actually a third masculine plural pronominal suffix, similar to the first clause (“their best”). The line would read יְשָׁרָם מְסוּכָה (yesharam mesukhah) “their upright person is a thorn bush.”

*Text-critical note:* The text is uncertain at several points. Where the MT reads יוֹם (yom, “day [of]”), the LXX reads οὐαὶ (ouai, “woe”) implying הוֹי (hoi, “woe”). The watchmen may be actual sentries or symbolic of true of false prophets. If reading with the MT, the “day of your watchmen,” might be the day they are on the lookout for, or the day they have announced. Reading “woe” either warns the sentries on the lookout or rebukes false prophets.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “one who,” a substantival participle. The descriptions in the rest of vv. {{Micah 7:18|18-19}} fill out the rhetorical question, “Who is a God like you?” That is, they provide descriptions of God as reasons that make him without equal. This context uses two participles, e.g. “who forgives” and “who pardons,” and then independent clauses with third person verbs. A similar construction occurs in {{Psalm 113:5|Ps 113:5-9}}, with participles and a third person finite verb in v. {{Micah 7:7|7}}. Here, making the two participles grammatically dependent on the rhetorical question and then switching to the third person is confusing English style. It masks that all these descriptions are serving the same function as a list of unique qualities of God, who is addressed in the second person. To tie these together in English, all the descriptions can be made into second person statements (so NIV), though this does not clarify the distinction of when the original text deliberately switches back to second person in v. {{Micah 7:20|20}}. Another approach would be to translate the third person clauses as indefinite and dependent, e.g. “Who is…like you, someone who does X, someone who does Y?” Or the interrogative force can be be extended, e.g. “Who is the one who does not stay angry?”

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads וְתַשְׁלִיך (vetashlik, “and you will throw”), while the LXX, Syriac, and Vulgate read “he will throw,” implying וְהַשְׁלִיך (vehashlik). Being conceptually tied to the previous verb, this one should be part of the list begun in v. {{Micah 7:18|18}}, so the third person form is expected. Also the vav plus perfect consecutive is more typical than vav plus imperfect in this setting.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “their sins.” The LXX, Syriac, and Vulgate read “our sins.” The shape of the letters in the first person plural suffix נו (nun and vav) look very much like ם (a final mem), which makes the third person plural suffix. Confusing the two is not an uncommon copying error. It may also be an enclitic ם rather than a pronominal suffix. In that case the suffix from the preceding line (“our”) may be understood as doing double duty.

*Study note:* In this metaphor the Lord disposes of Israel’s *sins* by throwing them into the waters of the *sea* (here symbolic of chaos).
